title: Quantifiers and determiners in context
objectives: Choose quantifiers for countable and uncountable nouns.
Distinguish few and little from a few and a little.
Use every and each with singular nouns.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Quantifiers describe how much or how many of something we mean. The noun's form matters. We use many and a few with plural countable nouns: ‘many books’ and ‘a few books’. We use much and a little with uncountable nouns: ‘much time’ and ‘a little time’. Countable nouns have singular and plural forms; uncountable nouns such as information and furniture normally do not take a plural in these meanings.

A lot of can be used with both plural countable and uncountable nouns: ‘a lot of people’ and ‘a lot of water’. It is common in positive statements as well as questions and negatives. Much is especially common in questions and negatives in everyday English: ‘How much time?’ and ‘I don't have much time’. It also occurs in other contexts.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Use how many with a plural countable noun: ‘How many chairs do we need?’ Use how much with an uncountable noun: ‘How much milk is left?’ The answer may give an exact number or a general quantity. Some and any can also be used with countable plurals and uncountable nouns: ‘some chairs’, ‘some milk’, ‘any chairs’ and ‘any milk’.

A few means a small number and is often more positive than few: ‘We have a few chairs’ says there are some. ‘We have few chairs’ emphasises that the number is small, often too small for a purpose. Similarly, a little means a small amount, while little often emphasises scarcity: ‘We have little time’. Context determines the implication.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘There are a few biscuits, so we can share them’ with ‘There are few biscuits, so some people may not get one’. The first focuses on the fact that some exist; the second highlights a shortage. Compare ‘I have a little time, so I can help’ with ‘I have little time, so I cannot help for long’.

Every and each generally take a singular countable noun in these patterns: ‘Every student has a ticket’ and ‘Each student has a ticket’. Each often focuses on members individually; every often presents them as a group of individual members. Their uses overlap, but they are not identical in every context.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use many with an uncountable noun in the usual quantity pattern: say ‘much information’ or ‘a lot of information’, not ‘many informations’. Do not use much directly with a plural countable noun: say ‘many chairs’ or ‘a lot of chairs’. Some nouns can be countable in one meaning and uncountable in another, so consult the context.

Do not assume few and a few have exactly the same effect. Both describe a small number, but the presence of a often changes the emphasis. Similarly, ‘not much’ and ‘a little’ can overlap in quantity while presenting it differently. Choose the form that matches the speaker's intended message.

common_errors.incorrect: How much chairs do we need?
common_errors.correct: How many chairs do we need?
common_errors.reason: Use many with plural countable chairs.

common_errors.correct: We have a lot of information.
common_errors.reason: Information is uncountable in this meaning.
Every takes a singular countable noun and singular verb in this pattern.

summary: Use many and a few with plural countable nouns; use much and a little with uncountable nouns.
Few and little often emphasise scarcity; a few and a little present some as available.
Every and each generally take a singular countable noun in the patterns taught here.
